articles.text: Piedmont City Council was given an update on the Piedmont Community Pool project and approved a $100,000 for soft costs at their Council meeting on Monday, August 4. According to project leaders, the new pools are expected to be filled with water in the last week of August, which will be followed by 6-8 weeks of system testing known as “commissioning.” The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU. The reallocated funds account for special inspections and testing, a mandated safety measure, as well as design services moving forward. “This still falls within our total project budget,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We think we have a firm understanding of what the hard costs are, and we are moving some of the budget we had allocated [previously] to the soft cost. So it’s like taking from one pocket and putting it in the other.” As of July 30, construction was estimated at 96% complete. The project crossed a milestone on Thursday, July 31, as crews completed the final concrete pour for the activity pool deck, pedestrian bulb-outs at the Magnolia/Bonita intersection, and a sidewalk leading into the pool entrance from Bonita Avenue. articles.text: After nearly two years of public engagement, AC Transit is announcing new changes to their bus network, with changes going into effect on Sunday, August 10. The route changes will discontinue extended school-hour service connecting the Hampton/ Estates Drive area to Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary School. “We had been, for a year-anda-half, talking about the line in and service, and never did it come up that this school service might go away,” said Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen. A letter was sent to AC Transit to express dismay at this change to Piedmont’s bus service, which could have an effect on students. The letter was sent by Mayor Betsy Andersen, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, and School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. “This vital school-hour service provides the sole transit connection to local schools for a significant portion of the 1,700 students attending school in the Piedmont civic center,” reads the letter. “Discontinuing this service significantly impacts these students’ access to safe transportation to school and places undue burden on families, especially those with working parents who are unable to provide transportation during school commute times.” The upcoming changes include the removal of the existing line 33, and its replacement with a new line 88 running between Piedmont and Downtown Oakland. “Every decision was guided by three core principles – reliability, equity, and frequency,” said AC Transit External Affairs Representative Maria Henderson in an announcement at Monday’s City Council Meeting. According to Henderson, the new planned bus routes aim to respond to changes in travel patterns since the COVID-19 Pandemic. A full list of changes to all AC Transit bus routes can be found at actransit.org/realign. As long as I was throwing lobs to Lebron and KD, I wouldn’t even have to be that good. 1700th Anniversary of Nicene Creed By Pastor Jim Hopkins We Baptists are given to identifying ourselves as “non-creedal’ people, (we like to say that we have no creed but Christ and that the Bible is our only authoritative written word). But even Baptists of long standing, like myself, must admit that the 1700th anniversary of a historic Christian creed is worthy of notice. Seventeen hundred years ago more than 300 bishops and officials participated in the first ecumenical council of the Christian church. It met between May and August 325 in the Byzantine city of Nicea (now Iznek, northwestern Turkey). The council was convoked by Emperor Constantine (r 306-337) to address the Arian controversy that threatened the unity of the early church, and for Constantine who viewed Christianity as the cement of his empire, the health of the empire itself. Using beautiful, majestic and lyrical language – We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father. - the Council rejected the Arian argument that the Son was somehow secondary to the Father and provided language that is still used by Christians around the globe to affirm their faith during worship and to define their faith in the public square. It is less well known that the first Nicene Council also took action to set the date of Easter as the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox. It was a consequential gathering to say the least. As a non-creedal Christian one of the things I value, apart from its longevity, beauty and enduring impact, about the Nicene Creed is its focus on Jesus the Christ as the very heart of the Christian faith. In contrast to many contemporary statements of faith, the creed does not mention the Bible as a focus of belief. Instead, it devotes the great majority of its words to the identity and work of Jesus. In the creed it is Jesus, rather than the Bible, that is the eternal Word of God. articles.text: A Piedmont resident learns about Planning & Building projects at an open house event earlier this year. The City of Piedmont will host an open house to get residents to meet city staff and learn about various projects related to housing development, sustainability, and wildfire resilience. The open house will be held by the Planning and Building Department on Thursday, August 21 from 6:30- 8:30 p.m. at Veterans Hall, 401 Highland Avenue. The event will offer residents a one-stop opportunity to learn about upcoming projects and provide input before decisions are made. Residents may come anytime and move through five informational stations at their own pace. At each station members of the city staff will answer questions and provide details about project timelines. Featured projects include: • Moraga Canyon Specific Plan: A comprehensive plan for developing city-owned land along Moraga Avenue into a new neighborhood featuring affordable and market-rate housing, road safety improvements, and an expanded Coaches Field. • Objective Design Standards: Clear, measurable design rules that will govern new residential construction, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 developments. • Streamlined Business Permitting: Proposed zoning updates that will allow certain types of businesses to open through a ministerial process, avoiding a lengthy public hearing process. A resident has a conversation with a member of the City staff at an open house event. • • Building Electrification Strategy: A roadmap for how the City can support residents to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from their homes by replacing gas appliances with clean, electric alternatives. Building and Fire Code updates: Local amendments to state building codes to support wildfire-resistant construction and update Piedmont’s energy efficiency “Reach Codes.” This event is free, and no registration is required. Light refreshments will be served.

articles.text: A free performance of Shakespeare’s As You Like It is coming to Dracena Park on Sunday, August 10, at 4:00 p.m. presented by Vallejo Shakespeare Company. The performance will take place in the quarry area of the park with the rock wall providing excellent acoustics. Seating is first come, first served and will be picnic-style on the lawn. Community members are encouraged to bring a blanket or a low beach chair to enjoy the performance. Friendly, well-behaved dogs are welcome but must be on leash. Parking is limited on Artuna, Ricardo and El Cerrito Avenues. This performance marks the fourth appearance of Vallejo Shakespeare in Piedmont. Previous stagings include The Winter’s Tale (2023), Hamlet (2022), and Henry V (2019). Established in 2010, Vallejo Shakespeare Company produces one live show each summer, with free performances in outdoor settings across the Bay Area. The troupe uses minimal sets and costuming, putting the focus on the actors and the spoken words of the Bard. Vallejo Shakespeare Company put on a performance of Hamlet in Dracena Park in 2022. articles.text: In a show of collaboration between students, teachers and the school board, Piedmont High’s English Language Arts electives courses have been rescued from the chopping block and allowed to continue. During the May 14 School Board meeting students spoke during the open forum in support of Film as Literature, Public Speaking and Creative Writing, which were in jeopardy. When students were selecting their classes for this year, those classes were available and a healthy amount of students selected them. One of the two Creative Writing semester and the lone Film at Literature semester were under threat of being cut prior to the May 14 school board meeting. “The interest in these elective classes really is huge, it is a testament to just what Ms. Foster has done with students the past couple years,” said English teacher Elise Marks. “I have heard many students talk about how Creative Writing, Public Speaking and Film as Lit have made them feel human again, in a way they have lost since COVID. That they found community in those classes that they don’t find in their other classes, they have found their voices again, they have found passion,” said Marks. Mercedes Foster, the English Department chair, spoke in defense of the classes in jeopardy, and asked for the board to reinstate them. Twenty-nine students had signed up for Film at Lit, a class that the Post chronicled in an Inside the Classroom feature on March 15, 2023. Ella Hughes, a recent PHS graduate who will be attending Cal as a Comparative Literature major, spoke in staunch defense of the classes on May 14. “Cutting back on the course selection further than we already have, I know would materially impact potential career paths and interests for dozens of students,” said Hughes. “If you’re into English you just have the core curriculum, we can’t strip back over half the electives available in this area and not expect that’s going to seriously affect any students that are involved in the humanities,” said Hughes. Many students rallied to the lectern during the board meeting. “Humanities electives overall have prepared me for the future better than any APs or grad requirements,” said Sophena Tuli, a 2025 graduate. The passionate pleas of students and staff were heard, and in a show of collaboration those classes have since received funding and remain unhindered. “This one has a happy ending,” exclaimed Marks. “We’re delighted that the Board and superintendent agreed to fund an additional .2 FTE to enable all the students who signed up for Creative Writing, Public Speaking, and Film as Literature to take those courses.” Film as Literature teacher Mercedes Foster talks with 2023 PHS senior Teagan Haddawy about the day’s lesson on long-take, tracking shots.
articles.title: Language Arts electives to continue at PHS

articles.text: As the new school year quickly approaches, rising high school seniors who are college-bound should be finalizing their list of schools to which they will apply. Building a college list should consider a student’s academic goals, social needs and wants, and fit the family budget. Finalizing your college list should begin with a clear understanding of your budget. Use the Net Price Calculator for your intended schools to determine what you should expect to pay. If the anticipated cost of attendance is higher than what your family can afford, do not apply. It is heartbreaking to have a dream crushed by the reality of budget. Doing thorough research about each of your intended colleges should give you the information you need to determine if the school fits your academic goals. Ask yourself the following questions: Does it have the major you want to pursue? Are there opportunities for you to do research? How is the study abroad program, and can you still graduate on time if you do it? Do the schools align with your social needs? Know that there are fantastic colleges of all sizes! But knowing what your options are for residential living, extracurricular activities, intramural sports, or religious-based communities may all factor into your decision of whether a school is right for you. This research about social fit is important to make sure your time in college fuels your personal growth. College admissions are competitive for everyone- even high school valedictorians with perfect SAT or ACT scores don’t have a golden ticket. Your final college list needs to be balanced with regard to reach, target, and likely schools. Make sure that there are financial safeties in addition to academic safeties to avoid disappointment in the spring. Apply only to schools that you would actually consider going to. There is no use applying to more schools just to collect acceptances. Focus your attention and effort on schools you really care about and put forth your best application to each. Your time and energy are valuable. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. There’s going to be bumps in the road, and there’s going to be times for them to collaborate and times for them to reflect, and times for them to get ongoing training so they can build confidence around how to teach it,” said Fry. Fry cited one inspirational experience, with one of her 4th grade students in Berkeley, that solidified her career choice to be an educator. After the student’s mom moved out of state, Fry requested to continue with him in 5th grade by taking on his IEP. “The special education teacher said, you know, he’s very challenging. And I said, that’s okay, he’s a child. We’re going to love him, and we’re going to work with him through this. His father and his stepmother worked really closely with the special education team and me, and he made three years of growth in reading in one year,” said Fry. Fry described it as a beautiful experience. “When we can bring together the family, all the educators involved, and the student, we can all be in alignment and get on the same page to listen to each other. When we can work together, we can do incredible things for kids,” she added. Fry described this collaborative approach as an archetype for the work she wants to do as a principal. “It’s bringing together all the stakeholders in the child’s journey, really listening to everybody involved. Then, working collaboratively with that team to making sure you’re all communicating and on the same page so you can really help that child feel good about the progress that they’re making and their success,” said Fry about the work of a principal. Fry lives with her husband and two daughters in Alameda. Their oldest daughter will be a sophomore at University of Texas, and the younger will be a sophomore at Alameda High School. Fry’s willingness to be open promises to bode well for her and everyone at her new home, Wildwood Elementary. Don’t be shy; come in and say hi to Principal Fry. articles.text: Four Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 returned to the East Bay last month after completing an unforgettable 8-day, 7-night backpacking expedition through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains – a journey that tested their endurance, fostered camaraderie, and brought them face-to-face with some of California’s most awe-inspiring wilderness. Their journey covered over 70 miles on the trail under 40-pound packs and included over 15,000 feet of climbing. The group included brothers Miguel and Mateo Long, Sean Heafey, and Luke Ironside with adults Steve Long, Chad Ironside, and Bryan Houlette. Starting at the 10,200 foot Cottonwood Lakes Trailhead outside of Lone Pine, the Scouts traversed 12,178 foot New Army Pass and settled into their third night of camp at Timberline Lake, where alpine serenity and crisp mountain air rejuvenated their spirits. From there, they tackled the crowning challenge of their adventure – summiting Mt. Whitney, the tallest peak in the contiguous United States at 14,505 feet. Through wind, altitude and miles of switchbacks, they reached the summit with exhilaration and pride. On day six their route led them over Forester Pass, the highest point on the Pacific Crest Trail at 13,200 feet. The southern approach to this pass is dramatic, unlike any other pass in the Sierras. Originally deemed impassable by early trail builders, the pass was finally conquered in 1931 with creativity, determination, and of course, dynamite! One worker lost his life in its creation. A plaque at the site of the accident commemorates his sacrifice. Today, hikers are rewarded with panoramic views stretching north into Kings Canyon National Park and south into the vast Kern River valley flowing through Sequoia National Park. Each Scout was pleasantly surprised to find that parents had hiked in to meet them for the final night. Brendan Heafey, Sara Ironside and Marisa Strong brought new energy and gummy worms to the group. They fished and watched a beautiful sunset across Kearsarge Lake. The group exited via 11,760 foot Kearsarge Pass on day eight, exhausted but triumphant. Their journey was a physical achievement and a lesson in grit and gratitude. Through grueling climbs, freezing nights, starfilled skies, blisters, wind, rain, and thunderstorms, the Scouts returned with stronger leadership skills, tighter bonds, and stories they’ll carry for life. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 begin their 8-day, 70-mile trek through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains at the Cottonwood Lakes Trailhead outside of Lone Pine, California. Pictured are Steve Long (left), Chad Ironnside, Bryan Houlette, Miguel Long, Sean Heafey, Mateo Long, and Luke Ironside. An ancient Foxtail Pine, rare and remarkable is found only at elevations at or above 10,000 feet in California in the southern Sierra around Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks. They can live to be more than 3,000 years and are the second-oldest species tree still living on our planet. Troop 1 Eagle Scout Miguel Long shows the California State Fish and namesake of the wilderness that Piedmont Scouts traversed – the Golden Trout Wilderness. Golden Trout are world renowned for their brilliant coloration and high-altitude adaptations. They evolved in only two streams in the southern Sierra Nevada, although they have since been planted in hundreds of lakes and streams across almost every state in the Western United States. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 pause for a picture atop 11,760 foot Kearsarge Pass on the final day of an 8-day, 70-mile trek through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Pictured are Eagle Scout Miguel Long (left), Luke Ironside, Sean Heafey, and Mateo Long. articles.text: As I enter my senior year of high school, it’s the first question everyone asks. But why isn’t the question When do I want to go? Since I was five years old, I’ve spent every August to June in school. The schoolwork and stress that came along with it only worsened as I got older. Now, after years of spending my free time studying, college sounds exhausting. So, instead of jumping into more tedious lectures and late-night essays, a gap year sounds like a much-needed reset. For those who don’t know, a gap year is a break from formal education between secondary school and higher education. When my mom first mentioned the idea of taking a gap year, I immediately shot it down. I, like many others, believed that a gap year would only cause me to lose focus on my goals, fall behind, and appear less appealing to colleges. As it turns out, 60% of students return from their gap years with a more serious outlook on their academics. According to Denver Gap Year, this increased focus leads to gap year students scoring 23% higher grades than students who didn’t take a gap year. This increase in focus can boost a gap year student’s likelihood of being admitted to certain colleges. As a child, I was often asked what I wanted to be when I grew up. My answer never stayed the same. One day I’d want to be a doctor, the next I’d want to be an actress. At 17, I haven’t figured out my dream career path. Many of us don’t know what we want to do with our lives, but are asked to put something down on our college applications. This sort of uncertainty leads to 80% of college students changing their major at least once. Taking a gap year allows students to explore different fields of interest to discover what suits them best. Some may travel the world, develop an interest in a language, and choose to major in it. Some may intern at different businesses and find that they want to work in marketing. Others may paint and gravitate towards art history, or help animals and discover an interest in veterinary studies. Now, unable to decide, I’m planning a gap year that will test drive my interests. Maybe I’ll volunteer at a chimpanzee sanctuary in Africa to see if I want to study zoology. Or maybe I’ll coach tennis in El Salvador to see if I want to be a teacher. Everyone’s gap year can be completely different. It’s up to you. Taking a gap year doesn’t make me lazy or less than. A gap year allows me to dive into my passions, learn practical skills, and grow my perspective of the world. It’s about taking a step back to move forward with purpose. It’s a time to figure out who I am outside of the classroom. When I do enter college, I want it to be with a clearer sense of direction and a stronger understanding of who I am. Choosing what college I want to attend and, moreover, what kind of career I want to have are huge decisions. I want to make sure I make the best decision. For me.

With only so many end-ofyear awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost on the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on three athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in their largest role in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact included Kyla Williams in soccer and track, Massimo Mittone in baseball, and Savannah Dennig in basketball. Staff Photos KYLA WILLIAMS Soccer, Track and Field Kyla Williams is a rising sophomore and proved to be a spark on the soccer team in the winter and track as a sprinter in the spring. On the soccer team, Williams made a big impact as a forward, typically carving up defenses using her speed down the wing. She scored once in Piedmont’s NCS 5-1 win over No. 16 College Prep in the D4 playoffs. We gave her Athlete of the Week honors in January after scoring twice in Piedmont’s 5-2 regular season win over Castro Valley, while logging a goal and assist in PHS’ 4-3 loss to Alameda. With the track team, Williams earned an honorable mention for All-League honors. She reached the NCS Meet of Champions on the 4x100 relay team, which finished 17th of 24 teams. Massimo Mittone, a sophomore, is a standout pitcher on the baseball team. He didn’t give up a single run through his first four appearances and has established a 1.12 ERA in five appearances for a team-leading 22 strikeouts. He recorded two consecutive complete game shutouts, helping Piedmont win 1-0 over Miramonte on March 11 and 1-0 over San Leandro on March 20. Mittone was in consideration for our Freshman of the Year award before suffering a season-ending injury in late March. SAVANNAH DENNIG Basketball MASSIMO MITTONE Baseball Massimo Mittone has burst onto the scene for the baseball team last season as a freshman pitcher, building a 3-0 record in four starts. We named him The Posts’ honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in March. Savannah Dennig was another key member of Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team becoming one of the best in the state. She proved to be one of PHS’ best defenders, rebounders, and a reliable ball-handler. One of Dennig’s best performances came in the fifth-place final in the NCS Open Division against Salesian, where she put up 18 points and three rebounds in the Highlanders’ 70-48 win. She earned an honorable mention for All-League honors and our honorable mention for Freshman of the Year. Savannah Dennig was a standout freshman on the basketball team.

The United States remains No. 1 despite losing the 2023 World Cup in the Round of 16 to Sweden by way of penalty kicks. It’s a shame that the U.S. Women’s National soccer team doesn’t play in the CONMEBOL federation against the best South American teams like Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, and so on. This year’s Copa America Femenina’s final on Saturday, August 2 between the Canaries of Brazil and Los Cafeteros of Colombia played to a breathtaking penalty shootout, in extra time, with Brazil winning 5-4 after finishing extra time in a heated 4-4 draw. Colombia took the lead three different times, but the Brazilians answered after each score. Linda Caicedo opened scoring for Colombia in the 25th, but Angelina Alonso Costantino equalized with a penalty kick deep into first-half stoppage time at 45+9’. In the second half, Colombia forced an own goal on Brazil to take a 2-1 lead in the 69th minute, but Amanda Gutierres scored on a long-range shot for Brazil just 11 minutes later. With just two minutes of regulation time left, Mayra Ramírez put Colombia ahead at the end of a counter attack in the 88th. But Brazil wouldn’t go away. With the last kick of regulation, 39-year-old Brazilian legend Marta scored the tying goal at 90+6’ in stoppage time. Her shot was an absolute rocket from about seven yards atop the area, taking the attempt on her first touch on the volley. It was a breathtaking shot from Marta, leaving Brazil coach Arthur Elias with his head in his hands and tears of joy running down his cheeks. Colombia’s players stood in pure disbelief. Marta wasn’t done in extra time. In the 105th minute, she gave Brazil their first lead of the game after being left unmarked in front of Colombia’s net. Receiving a cross, Marta redirected the ball into the bottom corner. Then in the 115th with five minutes left in extra time, Colombia responded with another banger of a goal. This time, Leicy Santos arced in a free kick from a few yards atop the penalty area to force penalty kicks. PKs came all the way down. Brazil was once again on its heels after missing their second kick, but it was Brazil goalkeeper Lorena da Silva Leite playing the hero. Lorena saved a shot by Santos to keep Brazil ahead 3-2 despite their early miss, but Marta was stonewalled on the next attempt. With a 5-4 lead, Photo courtesy of Winchester Star Marta was Brazil’s Player of the Match, scoring two goals, including a stunning rocket from distance to force extra time. Photo courtesy of EFE.com Brazil’s goalkeeper, Lorena, made a pair of huge saves in penalty kicks to lift her team above Colombia.

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ current production of Terry Guest’s award-winning play The Magnolia Ballet has been extended through Saturday, August 16. The Magnolia Ballet is a southern gothic love story that explores themes of the Black experience, queerness, masculinity, and intergenerational relationships in the American South. Protagonist Ezekiel “Z,” a Black queer teen growing up in rural Georgia, builds a romantic relationship with his white friend, Danny. As their love grows, Z interacts with the ghostly ancestors of his past, including his father Ezekiel Mitchell V. Through these interactions Z reckons with homophobia, toxic masculinity and racism as he comes to terms with his own sexuality. The Magnolia Ballet, directed and choreographed by AeJay Antonis, made its Bay Area debut on the Shotgun Players stage last month. Guest’s play won the 2022 Jeff Awards for Best Production and Best Performer as well as the David Goldman Best New American Play Award. “The complexity of masculine love lies at the heart of this work. Fathers, sons, and friends navigate the razor’s edge between tenderness and violence, fear and vulnerability,” Marquis said in a press release. “Terry Guest writes about people like the men in my family who don’t always get a voice on the theatrical stage.” “He invites us in to see them,” Marquis added. “He doesn’t just make them villains. He cracks them open.” Shotgun Players Artistic Director Patrick Dooley said Guest also captures “that familiar sensation of the fine line between pain and love in our most intimate relationships.” “It’s so rare to read a play that seamlessly weaves poetic imagery and dances into a story with such a strong narrative,” he added. Jaiden Griffin stars as Ezekiel “Z” Mitchell VI with Drew Watkins as his father, Ezekiel Mitchell V. Nicholas René Rodriguez plays Danny Mitchell, Z’s best friend and lover. Devin A. Cunningham, who recently played the role of Juicy in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Fat Ham, takes on the role of the Apparition. Performances take place at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley, located at 1901 Ashby Ave. Tickets are available online at www.shotgunplayers.org/show/magnolia or by calling the box office at 510-841- 6500 x 303. articles.text: Concerts take place in the meadow on the Filoli historic grounds. Filoli Historic House and Gardens in Woodside launches its series of outdoor summer concerts, featuring six artists over two weeks, on August 17. Performances take place in the meadow on Filoli’s historic estate, combining nature, art and history for a truly unique Bay Area summer experience. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides for an idyllic backdrop to view the setting sun and enjoy live music on a pleasant summer evening. Gangstagrass, a hip-hop, country and bluegrass fusion band, launches the concert series on Sunday, August 17. Gangstagrass is the brainchild of founder Oscar Owens who had become an in-demand producer and singer/songwriter during the early 2000s. The group has released multiple albums since its formation, competed on America’s Got Talent and produced the Emmy Award-nominated theme song for the FX Network series Justified. All shows will run from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m., with check-in beginning at 5:30 p.m. The House and Garden will be open for guests to explore prior to the concert. To view a full list of performers, visit https://filoli.org/summer-stage/. The Summer Stage concert series coincides with Filoli’s Summer Nights events, serving as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden to the south. articles.text: The Napa Valley chamber music festival Music in the Vineyards’ (MITV) 31st season continues through August 24. Tickets are available for upcoming performances by Pacifics Quartet, Ariel Quartet and more. The series of live performances traditionally showcases distinguished chamber musicians as well emerging young talent during its four-week season in August, with concerts held at popular wineries and vineyards throughout the valley. With complimentary wine tastings at each intermission and breathtaking views of the Napa Valley, this unique combination of wine country ambiance and great musicianship allows audiences to experience chamber music in small intimate settings. The multi-Grammy award winning Pacifica Quartet performs next Wednesday, August 13, at Hudson Ranch and Ariel Quartet performs on Wednesday, August 20 at the Hudson House located at Beringer Vineyards. Pavone String Quartet, a group of undergraduate students at the world-renowned Shepherd School of Music at Rice University, perform on August 11. The Pavone Quartet are winners of Music in the Vineyards’ 2025 Fellowship Quartet competition. A finale concert is held on Sunday, August 24, closing the festival with Beethoven’s Archduke trio performed by a trio of virtuosos. A reception dinner under the stars follows. For more information on Music in the Vineyards and to purchase single day tickets, visit www.musicinthevineyards.org. articles.text: Vertigo, directed by Alfred Hitchcock, is, as anticipated, a classic psychological mystery-thriller that slowly draws the audience into its tightly scripted narrative from the first frame. Set in San Francisco in the mid-1950s, the story opens with Detective Scottie Ferguson (James Stewart) and a uniformed officer chasing a suspect across the flat, third story rooftops of a downtown building. Scottie slips and goes over the edge of the roof, barely managing to grip the roof’s gutter. Terrified, he is dangling above an alley, three stories below. The officer, leaning forward toward Scottie yells, “Reach up with your hand”…and suddenly he falls down to the concrete below. The impact of that moment results in Scottie developing vertigo, a fear of heights which can result in a disorienting feeling of falling or a fear of heights (aka agoraphobia). It forces the detective to retire from the department. This disabling fear is briefly demonstrated when Scottie visits his ex-fiancé, Midge (Barbara Bel Geddes), a fashion designer, who encourages him to stand on a stepping stool hoping he will, with practice, realize he is on the mend. This failed attempt only reinforces his sense of vertigo and a harrowing sense of losing his balance. The narrative then cuts to Scottie meeting with an old acquaintance, Gavin (Tom HelKim Novak and James Stewart in Vertigo more), a wealthy ship builder. After some minutes of small talk, Gavin explains that he is worried about his wife, Madeline (Kim Novak), who seems detached, acting strangely, seemingly fixated on her great-great grandmother, Carlotta. Gavin wants to hire Scottie, asking him to follow her and report back. At first reluctant, offering other alternatives (a psychiatrist), he agrees. All of the above is act one, slowly compelling; however, it is also the beginning of Hitchcock’s attempt to pull the audience into a perplexing mystery, one that fashions countless questions all while observing Scottie tailing Madeline. Her days include a visit to Carlotta’s grave where she places a small bouquet of flowers near the tombstone, and sits for hours in a museum, looking at an historical painting of this long-ago deceased woman titled “Carlotta.” To go any further would deprive the viewer of what I think of as a long and unexpected reveal; yet, this is, after all, Hitchcock. What is puzzling suddenly becomes a love story that takes a classic turn and stunning twist. Consider the title of the film, Vertigo, a condition which plagues Scottie. It becomes a metaphor for his obsessive need for Madeline while creating a sense of foreboding, which haunts the long and complex act three. Both Stewart and Novak are simply excellent. Both go through a metamorphosis regarding their characters and deliver exceptional performances. Vertigo. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock. Starring James Stewart, Kim Novak, Barbara Bel Geddes. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG. Released in 1958. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime/apple/Fandango. Sara Couden, contralto Zachary Gordin, piano

articles.text: The term B movie was long used to refer to those second tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature films. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, small budgets, and were the equivalent of those dime magazines widely popular during the same time period known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subjects running to gritty detective mysteries, wildly imagined tales of science fiction and melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B movie (and all the films of that ilk), it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. That’s not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plots and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. If it’s a truism that not all films have to be analyzed, or run through an intellectual colander, then B movies are a good fit. They are rarely ambiguous, or enigmatic or laden with the implied. Edge of Darkness uses the familiar and satisfying trope of revenge to move the plot along at an intense clip. articles.text: Lewis MacDougall in A Monster Calls A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-13. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of a gnarly yew tree, the British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar palliative, “happily ever after.” At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night, and coping with the life-threatening illness that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is also unable to turn to his rigid and distant grandmother (Sigourney Weaver). His father (Toby Kebbell) has been, for most of his life, absent, living in America and though he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, he offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Objects begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him, insisting that he tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to suspend his disbelief, yet boldly resistant to what is but cannot be. And so, just after midnight the monster returns and shares with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor. And, as the monster points out, each contradictory, for, as the monster explains, they are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him and there is nothing he can do. Together the two of them cling to hope: his that she will live, that each new treatment will be a cure. Hers that she can prepare her son for what she knows will be. And Conor, deeply conflicted, rages against the arc of his mother’s decline, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative. And it never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. While it could have dropped into a well of melodrama it instead grasps life and looks at both its darkness and light and searches for a truth that is often absent from such stories. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that is asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Directed by J.A. Bayona. Starring Lewis MacDougall, Sigourney Weaver, Felicity Jones. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016. Now streaming on Fandango/ prime/apple tv/YouTube.

articles.text: Freaky Friday is a family friendly comedy, ideal for kids (8+), tweens and teens, but not to forget that parents will find lots to smile at as well. At the center of the story is single mom Tess (Jamie Lee Curtis), widowed several years ago and now on the brink of marrying Ryan (Mark Harmon). Her daughter, Anna (Lindsay Lohan), just 15, is a surly teenager. The two frequently find themselves at odds. Actually they couldn’t be more different. Tess is a multi-tasking, stressed-out psychologist, who either on her cell phone, checking her Palm Pilot, or seeing patients. Anna plays the guitar, is failing English, generally feckless and often in detention. One evening they go out for a Chinese dinner, the meal followed by a fortune cookie. While all seems benign, we soon learn that it wasn’t. Inexplicably, they wake up the next morning having discovered that they have, in effect, well, body-swapped. While it isn’t a new premise, as films go in Hollywood (recall Big with Tom Hanks, for example), Lohan and Curtis do a superb job trying to adjust to this remarkable change. Both stand before the mirror and have that expected “Good grief, what’s happened to me?” moment. Both actors are having fun with their roles, conveying that neither is prepared to walk in the other’s shoes. Tess can’t play the guitar, nor can she do algebra, nor navigate school. Anna stumbles through Tees’ neurotic patient appointments, and even attends a talk show where she tries to sell her mom’s recently published book on aging. Tess has a hilarious problem when she is confronted with the very awkward attention of Anna’s hunky, motorcycle riding boyfriend, Jake (Chad Michael Murray) who doesn’t want to take “no” for an answer. All of this amounts to one hilarious moment after the next, using the fulcrum word “empathy,” all while the story unfolds. Though they were both in constant disagreement, slowly they develop lots of insights into one another. Anna comes to understand what it means to be a mom, and Tess realizes that being a teen is no walk in the park, what with all the changes in moods that define what it means to be an adolescent. Reconciliation is not far off. Freaky Friday. Directed by Mark Waters. Starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Lindsay Lohan, Mark Harmon. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2003. articles.text: A series of paintings by Bay Area native artist Kristen Jensen is on display this month, with artwork depicting life during the COVID-19 pandemic. The exhibit, “Social Distancing – Five Years On,” is on display now through August 31 at Studios Eleven Gallery, 560 2nd Street, Oakland. An Artist’s Reception scheduled for August 16, from 1:00-5:00 p.m. Jensen has been painting professionally since 1999, and currently works from her studio at Studios Eleven in Oakland, California. Known for her abstract and representational art, many of Jensen’s paintings include architectural elements that hearken back to her childhood fascination with the blueprints her father Artist Kristen Jensen, a Bay Area native, paints in her studio. Social Distancing, No. 7: Masking Up. Depicted serving the Oakland community during the pandemic, Frederick Shavies would later become Piedmont’s Police Chief. Social Distancing, No. 11: College Life, 2020. Social Distancing, No. 4: The Ballet Lesson. Social Distancing, No. 12: Dreams Deferred. brought home from his architectural practice. Jensen’s work appears in private and corporate collections across the country. Notably, the gallery features a painting of Piedmont’s new Police Chief Frederick Shavies from when he was an officer in Oakland. During the early days of the COVID-19 shelter-in-place, Jensen met Shavies on duty in Oakland, and he kindly agreed to have his photo taken for her painting series. Navigating the fractures and polarization of 2025, Jensen’s painting series offers a space to revisit the unexpected moments of grace and collective perseverance during the COVID-19 pandemic. These paintings hope to reflect a shared experience, capturing the uncertainty, stillness, isolation, grief, resilience and unexpected beauty of those unprecedented times. “I started the ‘Social Distancing’ series as a way to stay connected to the outside world during the COVID-19 shelter-inplace,” said Jensen. “The subjects are mostly people I know or have seen my few trips out into the world, or images that have been shared by friends.” During the pandemic, Jensen used her project as a fundraiser to help people in the Bay Area experiencing food insecurity and kids in underserved communities. Prints and cards of the pandemic paintings were sold, with 100% of the profits going toward the fundraiser. Held every five years in Tallinn, Laulupidu is one of the largest choral gatherings in the world, bringing together more than 30,000 singers and tens of thousands of audience members in a multi-day celebration of music, identity, and cultural pride. For the youth of PEBCC Ensemble, it was an experience of a lifetime. Wearing concert attire alongside choirs from across Estonia, Japan, and beyond, Ensemble joined the Select Children’s Choir – a prestigious group made up of top young singers from Estonia – to perform advanced repertoire beyond the main festival pieces. Singing in perfect Estonian under the soaring arch of the Tallinn Song Festival Grounds, the same place where peaceful singing protests helped bring independence to the country decades ago, PEBCC singers rose to the moment with grace and power. Rain poured, trumpets blared, and the crowd erupted as the ceremonial flame was lit and tens of thousands of voices rose in harmony to sing Koit (“Dawn”) and the Estonian national anthem. “All of it was worth it for Ilus Maa,” said one singer, referencing the beloved closing anthem. Others described the moment as “magical,” “powerful,” and “absolutely unforgettable.” Photos courtesy of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir members Ava Tarapore (left), Georgia Orcharton and Ayla Montanez take part in the Parade of Flags event in Tallinn, Estonia. Grete-Maria Mihkelson of the Estonian TV Girls Choir (left) with PEBCC members Murielle Vance, Sophi Ouyang and Artistic Director Eric Tuan during the closing concert of Laulupidu song festival. The choir’s Estonian journey also included a cultural exchange with their host ensemble, the Estonian Television Girls Choir (ETV). Many PEBCC singers had previously hosted ETV members during the 2023 Golden Gate Festival in California, and the reunion was deeply meaningful. Together, they shared songs, meals, clapping games, and heartfelt goodbyes that had their Estonian hosts in tears. Before arriving in Estonia, Ensemble singers toured Finland, collaborating with Jyväskylä’s acclaimed Vox Aurea choir to perform Echoes of Eureka, a choreographed musical exploration of American identity written by Artistic Director Eric Tuan. From lake saunas to singing in centuries-old churches, the Finnish portion of the tour offered cultural immersion and camaraderie that set the stage for the emotional crescendo of Laulupidu. During the Great Depression in 1938 Tyson also make this land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled it with the intention that it would be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 1950s and 60s the land was a dusty, sometimes muddy baseball field for young kids. When grass was planted, youth soccer matches were often played there on a soggy field because an underground water flow was an on-going problem. Hampton Park has evolved greatly over the years. It is much different today than what Piedmonters experienced 100, 50, and even 25 years ago. A building was constructed in 2000 to house children's programs that is used by the Piedmont Cooperative Playschool and the Recreation Department. Dramatic improvements were made to the field and park during 2017 in a $2 million public/private partnership that the Piedmont community generously supported. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field more serviceable during the year. In 2019 the baseball backstop was dedicated and named in honor of Oakland Police Officer John Hege. The 41-year-old Piedmont native was one of four officers fatally shot following a traffic stop in East Oakland on March 21, 2009. He was the only one who remained alive long enough to enable his organs to be donated to people in need of transplants. articles.text: In 2003, Harvard undergrad and computer genius Mark Zuckerberg began work on a new concept that eventually turned into the global social network known as Facebook. Six years later, he was one of the youngest billionaires ever, and, for better or worse, he’s still filthy rich and still in the news. His fame got a bump in 2010 when the director David Fincher and the writer Aaron Sorkin made a movie about his rise and his travails. It’s called The social Network and you can catch it next week in Piedmont. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Social Network stars Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. Aaron Sorkin won an Oscar for his screenplay. The film was released in the United States on the weekend of October 1, 2010, debuting at Number One, with widespread critical acclaim. Rotten Tomatoes gave it an approval rating of 96%, followed by this critical consensus: “Impeccably scripted, beautifully directed, and filled with fine performances, The Social Network is a riveting, ambitious example of modern filmmaking at its finest.” Roger Ebert named it the best film of the year. “David Fincher’s film has the rare quality of being not only as smart as its brilliant hero, but in the same way. It is cocksure, impatient, cold, exciting and instinctively perceptive,” Ebert said. And Rolling Stone also named it the movie off the year, adding “ Fincher and Sorkin triumph by lacing their scathing wit with an aching sadness that defines the dark irony of the past decade.” In addition, the film appeared on 78 film critics’ top-ten lists. The Social Network will be screened on Thursday, August 14 at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. Everyone is invited on a drop-in basis. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunc. The next movie in the Piedmont series is Dead Poet’s Society, starring Robin Williams, to be screened on Thursday, September 11th.

Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking his long contemplated revenge) might have tried to kill him. As he looks for the killers (there were two), he begins to discover pieces to the puzzle that are at first perplexing but soon point not to him as the target but to Emma. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was flirting with the idea of becoming a whistleblower. Since this is pulp cinema, there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) wherein the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hardedged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s persona throughout the film.

articles.text: On Monday, July 28, at 2:25 pm, an armed robbery occurred in the 100 block of Arbor Drive in Piedmont where suspects stole tools from construction workers at gunpoint. Piedmont Police officers responded and began an investigation which later led to the arrest of four suspects in Oakland and the recovery of a firearm. The two victims were working inside an unfinished garage on Arbor Drive when a black Nissan Altima approached and two men got out. One suspect pointed a firearm at the workers and ordered them not to move while demanding their tools. A victim reported both suspects were armed. A toolbox and a table saw were stolen and then the suspects fled on foot back to the Nissan. A third suspect, who had remained in the driver’s seat, drove away. Just after 7:00 p.m., Piedmont Police officers Singh and Faucher located the suspect vehicle in Oakland on Fruitvale Avenue. It is relatively easy to critique the creed on the basis that it was written exclusively by males, that the theological debates it tried to resolve seem rather insignificant to people of a much later time and place and that any effort to put the faith into words is by definition incomplete and inadequate. Still, meaningful cultural exchange and unforgettable memories. But it was Tallinn, and Laulupidu, that brought everything into focus. From spontaneous singing on the grass to processions through the rain-soaked streets of Old Town, PEBCC singers experienced firsthand how song can unite generations and nations. “The moment the flame was lit and the whole crowd began singing, I understood what this meant to them,” said one singer. “I’ll never forget it.” As PEBCC looks ahead to future exchanges, including its own Golden Gate Festival in July 2026, the lessons of Laulupidu will continue to resonate: that music has the power to transcend language, to carry history, and to forge lifelong friendships. Former boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan departed the school in 2024 as its most successful soccer coach of all time. New coach, Ben Russell, went 13-4-9 (W-T-L) overall in his first season toward a D4 NCS Finals appearance and the D4 CIF NorCal title. Girls’ soccer has routinely competed in NCS, but are coming off a questionable decision to fire head coach of nearly 20 years, Dan Chubbock—throwing some question into how the successful legacy of girls’ soccer will continue in Piedmont.
